tier_reason: doc/benchmarks.md compares flatcc's C output with Google flatc-generated C++ on the flatbench schema, and the benchmark code is public (test/benchmark/benchflatc/run.sh, test/benchmark/benchflatcc/run.sh, driven by scripts/benchmark.sh). Flags (-O3 -DNDEBUG) and CPU (2.2 GHz Haswell Core i7) are stated, but the compiler is never named or versioned (scripts just call the system `cc`/`c++`), so this is first-party with partial methodology: C, not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Encode: flatcc 626.074 ns/op vs flatc C++ 701.606 ns/op, about 1.12x faster (derived from page data). Decode/traverse: flatcc 28.652 ns/op vs flatc C++ 28.866 ns/op, effectively tied (~0.7%, derived from page data). The page itself says flatc and flatcc 'are close enough in performance for it not to matter much' and that flatcc's encode edge is 'likely due to less memory allocation'.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Compiler not named or versioned: the scripts use the system-default `c++` (CXX) with -O3 -DNDEBUG -std=c++11 for the flatc C++ build and `cc` (CC) with -O3 -DNDEBUG -std=c11 for the flatcc C build (test/benchmark/benchflatc/run.sh, test/benchmark/benchflatcc/run.sh).
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark (run and published by the flatcc maintainer); the compiler vendor/version is never stated, so it falls short of Tier A. The numbers are old: doc/benchmarks.md content dates from 2015-2016 (last content change 2016-02, moved to its own doc 2017-07) and has not been refreshed against current flatc/flatcc. test/benchmark/README.md says allocation strategies differ (the C++ builder is constructed on every iteration while the C builder is reset), which the page itself credits for flatcc's encode edge. The repo's raw Ubuntu run (test/benchmark/benchout-ubuntu.txt) reverses the encode result: flatcc 531.227 ns/op vs flatc C++ 515.662 ns/op (flatcc ~3% slower), while decode is flatcc 27.539 vs 29.967 ns/op (~8% faster). Overall the win over FlatBuffers C++ is marginal and platform-dependent.

notes: Numbers on the page match the record exactly; the ratios are correctly marked as derived. Downgraded A to C only because the compiler is unnamed (the record's own caveats admitted this); metadata (Apache-2.0, 769 stars, last commit 2026-09-25, not a fork, not archived) all check out.

tier_reason: benchmarks.md compares the msgspec_serde generated API with the official Python FlatBuffers Object API using public pyperf code (benchmarks/benchmark.py, benchmarks/_suite.py, benchmarks/run_pinned.py) on a stated Intel Core i7-8650U with CPython 3.13.5 and pinned package versions. The measured speed comes from a Rust pyo3 extension (rust/, built by maturin with profile=release), and no rustc version is stated. That is first-party with partial methodology, so C, the same as the orjson precedent.

The chart on the same page (benchmarks/images/python-flatbuffers-comparison.png, small/medium/large profiles) shows slightly lower figures: encode 18.7x/21.8x/20.7x, decode-to-model 10.6x/11.8x/11.6x, selected fields 1.2x/1.2x/1.3x, full traversal 1.4x/2.5x/2.8x.
corrections.workload: Official-API comparison: a FlatBuffers 'Monster'-style schema at three profiles (small 100, medium 5,408 and large 1,118,720 logical elements), measuring encode of a materialized model, decode to a materialized model, lazy-view selected-field reads and lazy-view full traversal, with pyperf (6 processes x 5 values) on one isolated core. The separate 1,000-object File/Directory graph benchmark (16- and 256-value NumPy vectors) compares msgspec/orjson/ormsgpack and msgspec-serde's own JSON, MessagePack and FlatBuffers codecs, not the official FlatBuffers API.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: CPython 3.13.5; msgspec 0.21.1, NumPy 2.5.2, Python FlatBuffers 25.12.19, flatc 23.5.2, msgspec-serde 0.1.0. The speed-critical path is a Rust pyo3 extension built by maturin with profile=release (pyproject.toml, rust/Cargo.toml, edition 2024); the rustc version is not stated.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 1 star (repo created 2026-08-25; v0.1.0 and v0.1.1 released 2026-08-30)
corrections.caveats: Baseline is the official pure-Python FlatBuffers binding (interpreted-language overhead), not FlatBuffers' native C++ core, so the win mostly reflects Python API overhead rather than a beat of the FlatBuffers C++ engine. The benchmarks.md prose rounds up slightly compared with its own chart (for example encode 18.7x-21.8x in the chart vs '20–22x' in the text). The measured speed comes from a Rust extension whose rustc version is not stated. The benchmark is first-party, on a single machine/CPU model. The project is brand new (1 star, created 2026-08-25). tier_reason: The README section gives one first-party headline ('up to 76% better than protobuf at merging two records') plus two bar charts for merge and projection at sizes 1/5/10, with no compiler, flags, CPU or protobuf version stated. The Criterion code that produced the charts (benches/src/serialization.rs vs prost 0.12, added in PRs #11/#16) was deleted from HEAD in PR #31 and survives only in git history, so C.

corrections.baseline: Protobuf (Rust prost 0.12 implementation, per the since-removed benches/Cargo.toml)
corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'Imprint performs up to 76% better than protobuf at merging two records', with Imprint merge time roughly constant while protobuf grows with record size. Merge chart (approximate read-off): protobuf ~1000 / ~2140 / ~3450 vs Imprint ~785 / ~800 / ~800 at merge_size_1/5/10, so ~4.3x at the largest size (derived from page data, approximate). The projection chart has no ratio in the text. It shows Imprint SLOWER at project_size_1 (~580 vs protobuf ~360) and faster only at size 5 (~650 vs ~890) and size 10 (~625 vs ~1530) (approximate read-off). The chart's y-axis unit is labeled ambiguously as 'ns/µs'.
corrections.workload: Criterion micro-benchmarks on fake Product/Order records at sizes 1, 5 and 10. Merge: decode two records and write an enriched combined record (protobuf: prost decode of both, clone into an EnrichedOrder, re-encode; Imprint: read both, directory merge, write). Projection: read one record and write a field subset (protobuf: decode and re-encode a SimpleProduct; Imprint: project 6 fields and write).
corrections.caveats: The README shows only chart images plus one headline percentage. Compiler/toolchain, flags and CPU model are not stated. The baseline is Rust prost 0.12, not Google's C++ protobuf. The protobuf comparison harness (benches/src/serialization.rs, benches/Cargo.toml with prost 0.12) was removed from the repo in PR #31 (2025-05-28): the current benches/serde_bench.rs benchmarks Imprint alone, so the charted comparison is reproducible only from git history (commit f42484cf). The protobuf merge path also clones both decoded messages, which adds allocation to the baseline. Imprint is slower than protobuf for projection at the smallest record size. Last commit was 2025-07-15, over a year ago.

notes: Headline 76% merge figure matches the README and the chart. Tier C stays, but the record's statement that serde_bench.rs is the public comparison code is wrong: that file has no protobuf path, and the prost-based harness exists only in history. Metadata (MIT, 170 stars, last commit 2025-07-15, stale, not a fork) checks out. baseline_in_list left unchanged; the orchestrator should note the baseline is prost, not Google protobuf.
